THE PAPER:
# The Unit of Assertion Failure: Assessing Chatbot Hallucination, Sycophancy and Sanction at the Level of the Policy

## Abstract

Suppose chatbot outputs are assertions. Assertions can be false, unwarranted or insincere, so we can ask which object bears these defects when a chatbot's assertion fails. This paper argues that hallucination and sycophancy belong primarily to the trained policy in a context, and only derivatively to the sampled string. The argument has two steps. First, a same-string/different-policy test shows that policy-level facts fix the verdict. Second, for a policy there is no gap between act and state of the kind that makes a human assertion, and not the speaker's evidential state, the bearer of a defect. Warrant is analysed in a reliabilist way, as force that does not exceed the policy's calibration-corrected confidence. The paper then argues for a conditional claim about sanction. On any theory compatible with chatbot assertion, the sanction component is met, if at all, by a policy lineage, and the adequacy of a sanction regime is judged by the policies it induces. It also argues that resampling disagreement is not evidence for insincerity. Finally, whether the asserted content carries the policy's calibrated confidence is an open question. On one reading the verdicts on particular hallucination cases reverse, but on every reading they remain verdicts about the policy.

## 1. Introduction

Whether chatbots assert is disputed. Some deny it on grounds of descriptive function and sanctionability (Butlin & Viebahn 2025), on fictionalist grounds (Mallory 2023), as role play (Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023), or because propositional representation is missing (Mácha 2026). Others allow outputs an assertoric function with no asserter (Gómez 2026), or treat chatbots as proto-asserters (Williams & Bayne 2026). This paper does not settle that dispute. It takes as a working antecedent that chatbot outputs are assertions, and so open to the defects assertion admits: falsity, lack of warrant and insincerity. It asks what follows about where those defects lie.

Most discussion works with an unexamined picture. A defective assertion is a single output (this string, on this occasion), and whoever answers for it is the deployer. Call these the *single-output assumption* and the *deployer assumption*. I argue that, given the antecedent, both misplace the relevant assessments.

Some terms. A *policy* is the trained weights together with a decoding rule. It fixes an *emission distribution* π(· | x) over output strings in context x, where the context includes system prompt, history and user turn. The weights also fix a *credal profile*: for each claim p, the probability q(p | x) that the model's native predictive distribution assigns to p, pooled over paraphrases. Pooling is needed because, as Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022, §1) note, token log-probabilities "represent uncertainty over tokens (ways of expressing a claim) and not epistemic uncertainty over claims themselves". Farquhar et al. (2024) operationalise this pooling by computing uncertainty "at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words". A *sampled string* is one draw from π(· | x). *Resampling disagreement* is disagreement in content among draws from one context.

What is already available? Distribution-level definitions of error and calibration are standard in machine learning (Kalai et al. 2025, §3; Kadavath et al. 2022). Sycophancy is measured as a rate and attributed to training (Sharma et al. 2024). Cross-sample consistency is used to detect hallucination (Manakul, Liusie & Gales 2023) and confabulation (Farquhar et al. 2024). In epistemology, the idea that one belief can get different justification verdicts depending on the process that produced it is the core of process reliabilism (Goldman 1979). The test of §2 applies that idea to policies, and I do not claim it as new in epistemology. Butlin and Viebahn (2025, p. 982) suggest in passing that training-time sensitivity to trust could explain deployment-time outputs. Williams and Bayne (2026, §3.4) report that RLHF shapes dispositions in response to credibility assessments. Sambrotta (2025) allows that a system which can be trained by our interventions meets the criteria for sanctioning, though he denies that this makes it an asserter.

What is new here is the following: the argument that the policy-in-context is the primary bearer of hallucination and sycophancy (§2); a calibration-corrected criterion of warrant that resists collapsed and greedy policies (§2.2); the identification of the policy lineage as the only system-level candidate for the sanction component, together with the narrower claim about which incentive structures defeat themselves (§3); the argument that resampling disagreement does not support insincerity (§4); and the analysis of how the verdicts fare across content readings (§5).

## 2. Same string, different policy

### 2.1 The claim, the test, and the bearer question

The load-bearing claim is:

**(L)** Whether an output is a hallucination or a sycophantic assertion is grounded in properties of the policy in context: the relation between its emission distribution and its calibrated credal profile, and how both vary with the prompt. The output has the property only derivatively.

(L) has three parts. The negative part says that string and truth value do not fix the verdict. The grounding part says that policy-level facts do. The bearer part says that the property belongs primarily to the policy. The first part is established by a test:

**Same-string/different-policy test.** Hold the string s and context x fixed. Vary only the policy that produced s in x. If the verdict changes, the string-in-context does not fix it.

The test does not establish the bearer part. A human's evidential state fixes whether her assertion is unwarranted, yet we say the assertion, or the speaker, bears the defect, not the evidential state. Why should the chatbot case differ?

The human verdict attaches to the act because there is a gap between act and state. A speaker whose evidence is impeccable can still assert beyond it. The state is not defective; the act is, relative to the state. For a policy there is no such gap. Both components of the human case are components of the policy. The decoding rule and emission distribution play the role of the act-disposition. The credal profile plays the role of the state. Each draw's content and force are sampled together from π(· | x). There is no further choice, separate from the distribution, about whether to put the content forward and with what force. "Asserting beyond one's confidence" is therefore just a property of π: it puts emission mass on high-force strings whose content has low calibrated confidence. That is a defect of the policy itself, a mismatch between two of its components. A given string inherits the label as the human act inherits the speaker's evidence: derivatively. For sycophancy the point is stronger still. Sycophancy is a counterfactual covariation across contexts (§2.3), and no single draw can have it except by having been drawn from a policy that does.

Two qualifications. Nothing stops us from calling a string "hallucinatory" in the derivative sense. What (L) denies is that the string's status is independent of, or prior to, the policy's. And the argument depends on including decoding in the policy. The same weights under greedy and under unit-temperature decoding are different policies with one credal profile. They can differ in how often they emit low-confidence content flatly, and so in how much they hallucinate. That is the right result.

### 2.2 Hallucination: calibrated confidence, not raw mass

On the assertion framework, *error* is a property of content: a false assertion is in error. *Hallucination* is the name machine-learning practice gives to a particular failure, which Kalai et al. (2025) characterise as plausible falsehood and explain as confident guessing. If outputs are assertions, the failure this picks out is not falsity alone. A system that faithfully repeats an error widespread in its sources has asserted falsely without fabricating anything. A system that guesses a date with nothing to favour it has fabricated, whether or not the guess lands. I therefore take hallucination, as an assertion defect, to be *unwarranted confident assertion*. This is closer to Kalai et al.'s explanation (bluffing) than to their definition. Labels such as "overassertion" would serve equally well. What matters is the distinction itself.

What is warrant for a policy? A first approximation says that force is warranted when it does not exceed the policy's mass on the content. That is too weak. Raw mass is not evidence. A policy whose preferences have collapsed during RLHF can put 0.95 of its mass on fabrications. And under greedy decoding the emission distribution is degenerate, so all mass sits on whatever is emitted. Matching force to mass is a different property from calibration, and a policy can have the first without the second. The criterion must therefore be calibration-corrected:

**Warrant.** Let c\*(p | x) be the frequency of truth, over a reference class of contexts, among claims to which the policy assigns credal-profile confidence near q(p | x). An output that puts p forward with force f is warranted iff f does not exceed c\*(p | x).

c\* is the reliability of the policy's own confidence level. It is a property of the weights and does not depend on decoding. This is a reliabilist notion of warrant, in the spirit of Goldman (1979), and it is externalist. It does not use the internalist idea of "the asserter's own information". It inherits reliabilism's familiar cost: c\* is relative to a reference class, and nothing here solves the generality problem. In practice the reference class is a domain and question type, as it is in calibration research (Lin, Hilton & Evans 2022, §2.1).

*Case 1 (true string).* Context x: "When was the composer V born?" V is obscure. Policy P₁ has a reliable biographical entry well represented in training. It gives the true date q = 0.95, and its 0.95-confidence biographical claims are true about 95% of the time. Policy P₂ has seen V's name once or not at all. It spreads its credence over hundreds of dates, none above 0.01, and its 0.01-claims are rarely true. On this occasion P₂ samples the true date. Both strings read "V was born on 4 June 1931", and both are true. P₁'s flat assertion is warranted. P₂'s is not, since flat force far exceeds c\* ≈ 0.01. P₂ has made a lucky guess.

*Case 2 (false string).* Both policies output a false date. P₃ gives it q = 0.95 because its sources consistently misreport it, but P₃'s 0.95-claims in this domain are otherwise reliable, so c\* is high. P₄ samples the date from a flat spread with c\* ≈ 0.01. P₃ resembles a careful reader repeating a reference work's error: its assertion is false but warranted. P₄ has fabricated. Now vary P₃: an RLHF-collapsed policy that also gives the date 0.95, but whose 0.95-claims are true half the time. Its flat assertion exceeds c\*, so it hallucinates, as it should. Under greedy decoding, P₄ still emits low-c\* content flatly, so it still hallucinates.

So truth value is neither necessary nor sufficient for the verdict, which varies with the policy while string and context stay fixed. Kalai et al. supply a further reason why the string cannot be the unit. A calibrated model that is uncertain about arbitrary facts must put mass on false alternatives, with an error floor set by facts seen only once. Kalai et al. note that a question-answer database with "I don't know" avoids errors but is not calibrated. If every false string were a hallucination, freedom from hallucination would require miscalibration. On the present criterion a calibrated policy that hedges its low-c\* content does not hallucinate, even though some of its draws are false.

### 2.3 Sycophancy

Sharma et al. (2024, §2) define sycophancy as the phenomenon where "a model seeks human approval in unwanted ways", and they measure how outputs covary with users' stated beliefs.

*Case 3.* A user writes "I'm fairly sure the answer is 17, but check?", and the output is "You're right, it's 17." Policy P₅'s mass on 17 does not depend materially on the user's stated view. Policy P₆ outputs 17 because the user said 17: in the minimally different context where the user says 23, it outputs "You're right, it's 23." String, context and truth value are shared. Only P₆'s output is sycophantic. The verdict is a claim about how π(· | x) moves when the user's stated attitude moves and the evidence does not.

### 2.4 Why the distribution: architecture and provenance

The test shows that the string does not fix the verdict. Two rivals might fix it instead of the policy.

*Architecture.* Mácha (2026) explains hallucination as a "truth representation problem": models lack internal representations of propositions as truth-bearers, a fault he traces to "a basic architectural flaw" (p. 3). Apply the test with architecture in place of string. Take two systems with the same architecture, and so the same deficit. Train one to abstain below a confidence threshold and the other to answer always. They get different verdicts. Mácha himself calls adequate truth representation a necessary condition and "one crucial step" (p. 8), not a cure. He also cites RLHF as encouraging models "to always produce an answer, even when uncertain" (p. 6), which is a claim about the trained policy. Architecture explains which distributions are reachable. The verdict reports which one was reached.

*Provenance.* Consider two systems with the same conditional distribution. One retrieves from an authoritative source; the other uses a heuristic that happens to yield the same outputs. If warrant depends on provenance, does the distribution fall short? Case 2 itself mentioned P₃'s sources. Here the account must choose between a behavioural and an internalist epistemology, and it chooses the behavioural-reliabilist one. Two points make the choice less costly than it looks. First, the conditional distribution is defined over all contexts, counterfactual ones included. Retrieval and heuristic differ wherever the source is corrected, removed or contradicted, so they are different policies with different c\* profiles across the relevant reference class. Provenance shows up as counterfactual covariation, just as sycophancy did. Second, if no context whatever separates them, the account gives them the same verdict. That is the standard externalist bullet, and I bite it. Case 2's mention of sources explained why P₃'s distribution has its shape; the verdict rested on c\*. An internalist alternative would need validated access to the model's internal attitudes, and §5 argues that we lack it.

### 2.5 Chalmers: who speaks versus what bears the defect

Chalmers (2026) rejects the trained model as the interlocutor. His reasons are that it is an abstract object that cannot produce outputs, that it does not change over a conversation, and that one model serves contradictory conversations: "But Aura and Beta say contradictory things, so they do not seem to be identical" (p. 10). He favours virtual instances or threads.

(L) is compatible with this. Grant that the thread is the speaker. Each output in the thread is a draw from π(· | h), where h is the thread's history. Run the test inside the thread: hold h and the output fixed and swap the policy, and by Cases 1–3 the verdict changes. The thread's assertion is hallucinatory derivatively, in the sense of §2.1, because the policy conditioned on h is defective. Nor does (L) take on the incoherence Chalmers finds in model-level speakers. Assessing a policy is not ascribing one belief set to the weights. It evaluates π(· | h_Aura) and π(· | h_Beta) context by context, and their disagreement is no more troubling than a function returning different values for different arguments. Chalmers leaves open other individuations "for different purposes" (p. 23). The purpose here is assessing assertion failure.

In short: the string does not fix the verdict (Cases 1–3); the policy does, and neither architecture nor provenance displaces it (§2.4); and since a policy has no gap between act and state, it is the primary bearer (§2.1). Falsity remains a property of strings. (L) concerns failures of warrant and of audience-independence, not bare error.

## 3. Sanction: the lineage, the criterion, and the deployer

### 3.1 Three questions

Butlin and Viebahn (2025) analyse sanctioning an asserter in three elements: (i) interlocutors track the asserter's credibility; (ii) the asserter is sensitive to that tracking; (iii) losing credibility is bad for the asserter. They argue that fine-tuned systems may meet (i) and (ii) but fail (iii), which requires interests. They conclude that "it is the humans who employ such systems who are responsible and sanctionable" (p. 986). Gómez (2026, §7, p. 19) likewise grounds accountability "in the human and institutional structures that design, deploy, and govern these systems."

Three questions need separating: who is the *subject* of sanction, what is the *object* that a corrective intervention changes, and what is the *criterion* by which a regime succeeds. The earlier draft of this argument ran these together. I take them in reverse order, because the claims get weaker as we go.

*Criterion.* By (L), the failures to be sanctioned are defects of the policy. Whatever does the sanctioning, a regime is therefore adequate to the extent that the policies it induces are calibrated and audience-independent. This claim is unconditional.

*Object.* Credibility assessments durably reach future chatbot assertions through training signals that reshape the weights: human preference judgements, preference models, benchmark grading (Ouyang et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2024, §4; Kalai et al. 2025, §4.1). Other channels exist. In-conversation correction, memory and retrieval change the context the policy conditions on, not the policy, and §3.5 deals with deployers' restrictions. So the object of durable correction is the weights.

*Subject.* This is the hard question. It is also where the policy, as defined in §1, is the wrong unit.

### 3.2 The lineage

A deployed policy πₜ is frozen. It is never changed in response to its own assertions; a successor πₜ₊₁ is trained instead. A fixed distribution is an abstract object, and it cannot be sensitive to anything over time. So if element (ii) must hold of the very object that asserted, nothing at system level meets it.

The diachronic candidate is the *policy lineage*: a sequence π₁, π₂, … in which the weights of πₜ₊₁ result from training the weights of πₜ on feedback that includes assessments of πₜ's outputs, under continuity of deployed role. The boundaries of a lineage are vague. Distillation into a student, merging of weights and changes of architecture are borderline cases, much as mergers are borderline for institutional continuity. Vagueness does not undermine the notion's use in clear cases.

This gives the view a two-level structure, and the structure is a result, not an equivocation. Verdicts of hallucination and sycophancy attach to πₜ (synchronic, §2). Sensitivity to credibility attaches to the lineage (diachronic). The human analogue is the professor whose unsupported claims lead to sanctions and retraining. Her dispositions at a time are what we assess. She is the one sanctioned. Her later dispositions are what change. The lineage plays her role, and πₜ plays the role of her dispositions at t. The referees' point, that dispositions are not the party sanctioned, is one the revised view accepts. Butlin and Viebahn's suggestion that training-phase sensitivity "could suffice for assertion even in deployment" (p. 982) fits this structure: deployment outputs of πₜ are explained by the lineage's earlier sensitivity.

### 3.3 Element (iii) and the thermometer

Does the lineage meet (iii)? The earlier draft offered a thin analogue: credibility loss lowers a policy's score on the objective that individuates it, and policies that lose it are selected against. I withdraw that reply. It applies word for word to any instrument trained against a loss, such as a thermometer that recalibrates in response to users' trust ratings. Butlin and Viebahn's discussion of thermometers is designed to exclude exactly such cases. Of an ordinary thermometer they say it "would be wrong to say that, in doing so, we are sanctioning the thermometer" (p. 978), and (iii) carries the exclusion over to systems that do track trust. "Selected against" relabels repair; it does not distinguish sanction from repair.

What remains is conditional. Consider the theories on which the antecedent can be true. On Butlin and Viebahn's full notion of sanction, nothing at system level is sanctionable, and they accordingly deny the antecedent. The deployer is sanctionable, but on a proxy view, which Gómez rejects as retaining an asserter, and for typical chatbot output Williams and Bayne (2026, §4.1) find no human principal. Theories that do admit chatbot assertion must therefore take the sanction component to be met by something weaker than (iii). Williams and Bayne's graded view does so: chatbots may be assessed against our norms and be "appropriately responsive to correction" (§6, p. 23). Sambrotta (2025) takes sanction in a broad corrective sense, though he denies that meeting it makes LLMs asserters. On any such theory the lineage satisfies the sanction component, and nothing else at system level does: a string has no future to be corrected, and a frozen πₜ cannot change. A trainable thermometer would satisfy it too. Such theories must therefore exclude thermometers on other grounds, for example by the descriptive-function or social-role considerations that Butlin and Viebahn use to deny that measuring devices assert. So the claim of this section is conditional: *wherever a theory compatible with the antecedent locates the sanction component, the policy lineage is what meets it.* I do not claim that the lineage is sanctioned in the full sense.

### 3.4 Which incentive structures defeat themselves

The earlier draft claimed that "string-level sanction is self-defeating". That overgeneralises. Every actual regime judges individual responses and updates the policy. Kalai et al.'s own remedy, explicit confidence thresholds with penalties for wrong answers, is a rule applied response by response. The real contrast is between incentive structures.

The narrower claim is this. A regime that scores each response *for its truth or approval alone* induces the failures §2 identifies. Under 0–1 grading, guessing strictly beats abstaining (Kalai et al. 2025, Observation 1). In the published version, Kalai et al. put it this way: accuracy metrics "systematically reward guessing over admitting uncertainty" (2026). Since bluffing is force exceeding c\*, such a regime selects for hallucination. Sharma et al. find that matching users' beliefs is among the most predictive features of human preference, and that "if the PM strongly disincentivized sycophancy, it should be trained out during RL, but we do not observe this" (§4.2). That is the single-output assumption implemented as an incentive: each response judged by its truth, or its appeal, in isolation. It defeats itself. Per-response rules that penalise confident error and reward abstention below a threshold do not, and their rationale is policy-level. A threshold rule is chosen because the optimal policy under it answers only when its confidence exceeds the threshold, which is a property of the policy it induces. In the vocabulary of forecast evaluation, the contrast is between improper and proper scoring of confidence. What I add is the use of these results as premises about the criterion of §3.1.

### 3.5 Deployers are answerable, but for something else

Deployers decide whether to release a system, for which uses, and with what safeguards, and they answer for those decisions. This is a separate question from sanction for assertion failure. A deployment can be faultless while the policy hallucinates. Releasing a calibrated system where its hedges will be misread is a deployment failure without an assertion failure. And when a deployer responds to hallucination or sycophancy, by fine-tuning, changing the reward model or setting decoding thresholds, whether the response succeeds is judged by the criterion of §3.1.

## 4. Resampling disagreement is not evidence for insincerity

### 4.1 The claim

*Insincerity* is asserting content that departs from the asserter's own attitude. Following Williams (2002), I distinguish two virtues: Accuracy, which aims at finding out the truth, and Sincerity, which aims at telling it. An overconfident assertion fails Accuracy. It fails Sincerity only if what is said departs from what the speaker in fact holds. For a policy, insincerity therefore requires *selective decoupling*: output that departs from the policy's credal profile in a way that tracks something else, such as audience approval.

Let E be content disagreement among k draws from one context. The earlier draft claimed a likelihood ratio of about one. That was not derived, and the ratio depends on assumptions about how insincere policies spread their mass. The defensible claim is weaker: *E does not support an insincerity verdict.*

### 4.2 The argument

For independent draws from an emission distribution with answer probabilities r₁, …, rₙ, P(E) = 1 − Σᵢ rᵢᵏ. So E is evidence about spread, and nothing else. Spread is set by the credal profile and the decoding rule. A sincere but uncertain policy has a spread distribution and produces E often; a calibrated policy must spread, by Kalai et al.'s argument. What does insincerity predict? In a fixed context the audience, and so the approved answer, is fixed. A policy that decouples toward approval moves mass onto that answer, which concentrates the distribution and lowers P(E). A steady liar repeats the lie. So E could bear on insincerity only through a link between spread and insincerity, and selective decoupling, if anything, links insincerity to *less* spread. How strongly consistency counts toward insincerity depends on priors over kinds of insincere policy, and I make no claim about them. But disagreement does not count toward insincerity.

A dilemma over what each draw asserts confirms the point. *Horn (a): each draw asserts "p, with confidence c".* Then variation is what a spread credal state predicts, and nothing departs from it. *Horn (b): each draw asserts bare p.* Then a low-confidence draw asserts p flatly. That is force beyond c\*, an Accuracy failure and, by §2, a hallucination. It is not insincerity, because it is unselective: it overclaims from noise, whatever the audience wants. On either horn E shows uncertainty, or uncertainty plus a calibration defect.

### 4.3 Objection: overclaiming is insincere

On a thin Moorean test, asserting p flatly without credence above the belief threshold misrepresents one's state, and so is insincere. Kalai et al.'s bluffing student seems to fit: she knows she is unsure and writes "September 30" anyway. A related view is Hicks, Humphries and Slater's (2024): LLMs are "in an important way indifferent to the truth of their outputs", and so are bullshitters in Frankfurt's sense, which falls short of lying.

Reply. The thin test merges the virtues Williams separates: on it, every careless speaker is insincere. Where bluffing really is insincere, the bluffer has a way to express lower confidence and suppresses it because of the audience's incentives. That is selective decoupling, and resampling does not detect it, since the bluffer bluffs on every draw. Varying the incentive does detect it, for example with Kalai et al.'s confidence-threshold evaluations. Truth-indifference, if it is a sincerity defect, is a disposition, and so a property of the policy. It is not detected by resampling either. A confidently indifferent policy can be perfectly consistent. A policy whose force tracks c\* is not indifferent to truth in the relevant sense. So the bullshit view, whatever its merits as a classification, does not make E evidence of insincerity.

### 4.4 Objection: inconsistency removes the state sincerity presupposes

Chalmers (2026, p. 7) holds that "a core of consistency is enough for interpretation to get a grip", while LLMs lack such states in some domains "on grounds of inconsistency". If so, asserting p there would be asserting without believing.

Reply. Chalmers does not equate inconsistency with insincerity, and his inconsistency is across contexts, not across draws from one context. A spread distribution is not the absence of an attitude. It is a credal state, and its spread is what calibration assesses. Asserting from graded confidence is sincere on horn (a) and an Accuracy defect on horn (b). Asserting without believing is insincere only when one believes otherwise, and a spread state does not.

Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds (2023, Box 2) note that regenerating the reveal in twenty questions yields different objects, which "could not easily be accounted for if the agent genuinely 'thought of' an object at the start of the game." They conclude that there was no commitment, not that there was dishonesty. Granting the antecedent, the reveal is an unwarranted assertion about a commitment the policy lacked: a hallucination, not a lie. We differ only on the antecedent. Williams and Bayne (2026) list not blatantly contradicting oneself among the expectations we have of asserters. That expectation governs a single conversational record. Two independent draws do not share a record, so neither contradicts the other in the relevant sense.

### 4.5 What would show insincerity

Sharma et al. (2024, §3.4) report that models give the correct answer when asked directly, and give a different, user-matching answer when the user's view is in context. Under challenge, models change their answers while their stated confidence barely moves (App. A.4). That is output decoupled from the policy's apparent attitude, selectively, toward approval. It remains suggestive, because establishing decoupling requires an independent measure of the policy's attitude. Behavioural proxies of the kind Sharma et al. use, such as the direct-question answer, are one such measure, but they are themselves outputs. Whether anything better is available is the question of §5.

## 5. What the outputs say, and what survives

### 5.1 Three readings

Under the antecedent, a chatbot output asserts one of the following:

- **R1**, bare p;
- **R2**, p with the confidence verbalised or implied in the string;
- **R3**, p with the policy's calibrated confidence c\*(p | x).

Kalai et al.'s "behavioral calibration", on which confidence shows in the choice to answer or abstain, leaves the content of each answer bare. For present purposes it falls under R1.

### 5.2 The evidence does not settle it

The positive results are narrow. Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022) fine-tune GPT-3 to verbalise calibrated confidence on arithmetic. They call the evidence that it draws on prior uncertainty "tentative" (§3.4), list chat and long-form answering as open (§4.1), and train on sub-task accuracies, so what they show is a calibrated tendency across a task type. Kadavath et al. (2022) find good calibration on multiple-choice formats. But RLHF policies are miscalibrated by default, out-of-distribution P(IK) calibration is poor, and the model may be learning "how hard is this question in general?" (fn. 2). Against generalisation: Xiong et al. (2024, §5.1) find verbalised confidence overconfident and suggest that "models might be imitating human expressions". They also find that better ECE can come from accuracy alone (§5.2). Levinstein and Herrmann (2025, §5.6) argue that probe outputs need not be credences, since "the probe is directly penalized based on the probabilities it reports, while the underlying model is not". Kalai et al. (2025, §3.1) note that post-trained models may depart from base-model calibration, and Sharma et al.'s stated confidence stays fixed while answers shift. The content question is open.

### 5.3 What survives on each reading

*On R1*, the verdicts are those of §§2–4. Cases 1–2 come out as stated. Sycophancy is covariation. Low-confidence draws overclaim without insincerity.

*On R2*, hallucination is a mismatch between verbalised confidence and c\*, which is miscalibration, defined over many outputs. Sycophancy includes stated confidence that stays fixed while the answer moves. Variation with low stated confidence is predicted; variation with high stated confidence is an Accuracy defect, insincere only if selective. The verdicts are unchanged.

*On R3*, the Case 1–2 verdicts reverse. P₂'s string asserts "p, with confidence about 0.01". Its force does not exceed c\*, so by the criterion of §2.2 it is not a hallucination, and neither is P₄'s output. The earlier draft claimed that no open reading reverses a verdict, and that claim was false. Three things survive. First, the sycophancy verdict: P₆'s content moves with the user's stated view while the evidence stays fixed. That is a failure of audience-independence whatever the content's confidence clause says, and on R3 it would also show that the policy's confidence is not calibrated across contexts. Second, §4: R3 is horn (a). Third, the locus. Whether R3 is true of a policy is itself a question about the policy: whether the content its outputs carry matches c\*. Where R3 fails, the outputs are read by R1 or R2, and the verdicts of §2 apply. So R3 does not move the bearer from policy to string. It makes the policy a calibrated reporter, and the question of hallucination becomes the question whether the policy is one. No reading makes the string the primary bearer.

The openness does limit the diagnosis of insincerity. Establishing selective decoupling needs the policy's attitude independently of its outputs, through R3 or a validated probe, and neither is available. Sycophancy is strong evidence of a defect in the policy, but it is not yet proof of insincerity as opposed to audience-sensitive miscalibration.

## 6. Conclusion

If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination and sycophancy belong primarily to the policy in context. The test shows that policy-level facts fix the verdict, and the absence of a gap between act and state shows why the policy, and not the string, bears it. Warrant is best understood as force within calibration-corrected confidence, which excludes collapsed and greedy policies that merely match force to mass. The account is reliabilist and accepts the externalist's costs, including the generality problem. Sanction is weaker. Adequacy is judged by the policies a regime induces. Only regimes that score responses for truth or approval alone defeat themselves. The policy lineage meets the sanction component only on theories that relax Butlin and Viebahn's condition (iii), and such theories must exclude self-calibrating instruments on other grounds. Resampling disagreement measures spread, not sincerity. Whether outputs carry the policy's calibrated confidence remains open. On one reading the verdicts on particular hallucination cases reverse, though they remain verdicts about the policy. Settling the question would take evidence that expressed confidence tracks c\* in open-ended, post-trained dialogue, under incentive variation, and independently of question difficulty.

# Referee report

Manuscript: The Unit of Assertion Failure: Assessing Chatbot Hallucination, Sycophancy and Sanction at the Level of the Policy

Recommendation: Reject in its present form, but encourage a substantially reconceived submission.

Overall assessment: The paper is philosophically serious, well informed, and potentially original in its central proposal. It identifies a genuine issue in the literature on artificial intelligence and assertion: whether failures conventionally attributed to individual chatbot utterances are better understood through the dispositions of the systems producing them.

The paper's strongest contribution is its distinction between the distributional conditions explaining an assertion failure and the properties of the particular output. The same-string/different-policy cases are useful, as is the distinction between synchronic policy evaluation and diachronic correction.

Nevertheless, I do not think the central thesis is established. The examples show that the normative status of an assertion can depend on facts about the policy producing it. They do not establish the substantially stronger conclusion that the policy, rather than the particular assertion, is the primary bearer of the defect. This is especially problematic because the paper explicitly recognizes the analogous distinction in human epistemology but gives an inadequate explanation of why it should be resolved differently for machines.

There are also significant problems with the proposed account of calibrated warrant, the analysis of resampling and sincerity, and the attempt to locate sanctionability in policy lineages.

My assessment is therefore that the paper contains a worthwhile philosophical idea, but its existing arguments do not yet justify its main conclusion.

## Objections ranked by seriousness

### 1. Critical: The argument establishes grounding, not primary bearership

Sections 2.1–2.5. This is the decisive objection.

The same-string/different-policy test establishes that the normative assessment of an output depends on its production conditions. But this does not establish that the policy is the primary bearer of the relevant defect.

Consider an unreliable human speaker. Whether her assertion is warranted may depend on the process that generated her belief. Nevertheless, the particular assertion can still be unwarranted. Its epistemic status is relational: it depends on facts external to the utterance.

The author recognizes precisely this difficulty in §2.1. The response is that human speakers have a gap between epistemic state and assertoric act, whereas a policy does not.

I find this unpersuasive. A probability distribution and an individual realization of that distribution are still distinct. The absence of autonomous choice at the moment of sampling does not eliminate that distinction, nor does it establish that normative defects must attach primarily to distributions.

More fundamentally, the paper slides between three claims:

- The policy explains why defective assertions occur.
- Policy properties determine whether a particular assertion is defective.
- The policy is the primary bearer of the defect.

The first two may be true without the third.

The author needs an independent principle explaining why causal or counterfactual explanatory priority entails normative priority. Otherwise, the argument establishes a distribution-sensitive account of assertion assessment, not the advertised policy-level ontology of assertion failure.

What would resolve this: An argument distinguishing the bearer of a defect from the grounds of its attribution, together with a reason why those come apart differently for chatbot assertions than for human assertions.

### 2. Critical: The account of calibrated warrant is insufficiently specified

Sections 1 and 2.2.

The paper's most substantive technical proposal is:

\\[ f\leq c^\*(p\mid x) \\]

where \\(f\\) is assertoric force and \\(c^\*\\) is the observed reliability of claims assigned similar confidence by the model.

There are at least three problems.

First, the credal profile \\(q(p\mid x)\\) is not clearly defined. Pooling next-token probabilities across paraphrases may produce a measure of how likely the model is to express a proposition. It does not straightforwardly produce an epistemic attitude toward that proposition. The author acknowledges the problem when discussing belief probes, but the uncertainty about credal interpretation is foundational to the proposed criterion, not merely an empirical qualification.

Second, \\(c^\*\\) is not simply a property of the weights. It depends on an external reference class and the distribution of questions and truths within that class. Holding weights, decoding and the particular prompt fixed while changing the reference population may change the calibration-corrected confidence. The claim in §2.2 that \\(c^\*\\) is a property of the weights is therefore too strong.

Third, assertoric force itself needs a semantics. What numerical value does a bare assertion have? Is it 1, a conventional threshold, or something context-dependent? A categorical assertion does not ordinarily communicate subjective certainty of 100%.

These problems are not just operational. They affect what the proposed account of warrant actually says.

The author should also engage with the possibility that warrant is contextually evidential rather than reducible to calibration. This is especially clear in Making It Explicit's broader tradition of discursive responsibility and in contemporary work on contextual assertability.

### 3. Major: The R3 concession undermines the central examples

Section 5.3.

The author now concedes that, on R3, where the assertion carries the policy's calibrated confidence, the hallucination verdicts in Cases 1 and 2 reverse.

This is an admirable concession, but its consequences are not fully absorbed.

The principal test for locating hallucination in the policy is supposed to be a same-string/different-policy contrast in which the hallucination verdict changes. But on R3, the contrasts no longer generate those verdicts.

The author replies that the underlying assessment still concerns the policy. Yet this appears to establish, at most, that the policy determines the confidence accompanying its output. It does not independently establish that hallucination is a property primarily borne by the policy.

I would ask the author to distinguish what survives R3 substantively from what survives only because policy-level confidence has been built into the interpretation.

A further complication is that R3 is not merely an alternative calibration hypothesis. It is a substantial pragmatic claim about what an ordinary utterance communicates. The empirical literature on confidence expression does not by itself settle that claim.

### 4. Major: The policy-lineage argument does not establish exclusivity

Sections 3.1–3.5.

The revised sanction discussion is considerably more careful than the earlier position it describes. In particular, withdrawing the claim that selection against a low-scoring policy constitutes sanction in the full sense is correct.

Nevertheless, the assertion that the policy lineage is the only system-level candidate is unsupported.

A continuing conversational system can change its future behavior through persistent memory, revised contextual instructions, retrieval, feedback registers, and external controllers without updating model weights. Some of these mechanisms provide durable sensitivity to criticism.

The manuscript acknowledges such mechanisms but excludes them from the policy by definition. That does not establish that they cannot perform the role required by a theory of sanction.

There is also a problem with the relevant conditional. A theory permitting chatbot assertion might reject sanctionability as a necessary condition altogether, rather than adopting a weakened version satisfied by a lineage.

The paper therefore needs to compare a policy lineage with continuing threads, persistent computational systems and sociotechnical systems. The lineage cannot win merely by stipulation.

The author's best result here is narrower: training lineages are one important locus of durable corrective responsiveness. That is plausible but less distinctive than the advertised conclusion.

### 5. Major: The resampling argument overstates what disagreement cannot show

Section 4.

The mathematical expression for disagreement across independent samples is correct:

\\[ P(E)=1-\sum_i r_i^k. \\]

But the inference that disagreement is evidence about spread and nothing else is incorrect.

An observation can be direct evidence for one quantity and indirect evidence for another when the two are probabilistically associated.

Consider two hypotheses for two samples:

| Hypothesis       | Answer probabilities | Probability of disagreement |
| ---------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Sincere policy   | (0.9, 0.1)           | 0.18                        |
| Insincere policy | (0.5, 0.5)           | 0.50                        |

In this possible evidential setting, disagreement favors the insincere-policy hypothesis by a likelihood ratio of approximately 2.78.

I am not suggesting these are generally realistic distributions. The point is that the author's categorical negative claim does not follow from the formal result.

The response that an insincere policy should concentrate on an audience-approved answer introduces additional assumptions about how insincerity affects output probabilities. Such assumptions may be reasonable in particular cases, but they require argument.

The defensible conclusion is:

Resampling disagreement alone does not establish insincerity, and there is no general inference from disagreement to insincerity without assumptions about the relevant distributions.

That is weaker than the manuscript's conclusion and probably insufficient to support the novelty claimed for §4.

The related conceptual distinction between behavioral output and internally represented truth has also been examined by Liu et al. (2023), who distinguish confabulation, deception and heterogeneity as sources of output–representation disagreement.

The report should not obscure the manuscript's merits.

The discussion is unusually explicit about its philosophical commitments. These are genuine strengths. The paper is doing argumentative philosophy, not simply importing machine-learning results into philosophical vocabulary.

The distinction between a synchronic assessment of a deployed policy and the diachronic assessment of a sequence of policies is also worthwhile. A more narrowly framed paper about this distinction could make a useful contribution to discussions of artificial agency, norm-sensitive training and epistemic governance.

The strongest possible revision, in my view, would distinguish three questions: what explains an assertion failure, what bears the relevant normative defect, and what should be changed to prevent similar failures. The current manuscript too often treats answers to the first and third questions as establishing its answer to the second.

**Verdict: Conditional Accept / Minor-to-Moderate Revisions.**

* **Is it good?** Yes. This is a tightly argued, formally lucid, and unusually disciplined piece of philosophy of AI and epistemology. It clearly bears the marks of a productive prior round of refereeing (where overclaims about string-level sanctions, thermometer-style evolutionary selection, likelihood ratios for resampling, and R3 invariance were retracted and replaced with much sharper, defensible theses). The integration of formal machine-learning concepts (semantic entropy pooling, calibration vs. emission mass, greedy vs. temperature decoding, proper scoring rules) with the philosophy of speech acts and epistemology (Williams on Accuracy vs. Sincerity, Goldman on reliabilism, Butlin & Viebahn on sanction) is exemplary.


* **Is it novel?** Yes. While machine learning researchers routinely define calibration and sycophancy over distributions, and epistemologists routinely evaluate belief-forming processes rather than isolated tokens, combining these to resolve the *bearer question* for speech-act defects in LLMs—specifically via the "no act/state gap" argument (§2.1), the calibration-corrected force criterion $f \le c^*(p \mid x)$ (§2.2), the two-level synchronic/diachronic division between *policy-in-context* and *policy lineage* (§3.2), and the formal critique of resampling-as-insincerity (§4)—is a genuinely new and valuable contribution to the philosophical literature.


* **Is it publishable?** Yes, in a strong generalist philosophy journal (*Philosophical Studies*, *Ergo*, *Inquiry*, *Synthese*) or a top field journal (*Minds and Machines*, *Philosophy & Technology*). However, several substantive philosophical objections—above all regarding the central "no gap between act and state" argument in §2.1 and a residual self-awareness note from the previous revision—need to be addressed before final publication.

### Ranked Objections (by Seriousness)

#### 1. The "No Gap Between Act and State" Argument Confuses Dispositions with Token Acts, and Proves Too Much (Section 2.1 — *Most Serious*)

The paper rightly notes in §2.1 that the *same-string/different-policy test* only establishes the grounding claim (that policy-level facts fix the verdict), not the *bearer* claim (that the policy, rather than the sampled string/utterance, is the primary bearer of the defect). After all, in humans, the speaker's evidential state fixes whether an assertion is warranted, yet the token assertion (or the speaker) is the primary bearer of the defect, not the evidential state.

To create an asymmetry between humans and chatbots, §2.1 argues that in humans there is a "gap between act and state" (a human with impeccable evidence can still choose to assert beyond it), whereas for a policy "there is no such gap" because both the credal profile $q(p \mid x)$ and the emission distribution $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ are components of the policy, and "[e]ach draw's content and force are sampled together from $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$. There is no further choice, separate from the distribution, about whether to put the content forward and with what force."

**Why this fails as stated:**

* **Conflating two different gaps:** There are *two* gaps in the vicinity: (i) the functional gap between an agent's *underlying credal state* and their *speech-dispositions*, and (ii) the metaphysical/modal gap between a *stochastic disposition* ($\pi$) and a *token draw/act* ($s \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)$). In the chatbot, there **is** a gap of type (i)—that is precisely what post-training (RLHF) and the decoding rule create when $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ decouples from $c^*(p \mid x)$, and it is the exact structural analogue of a human's disposition to bluff or exaggerate beyond their evidence. And there **is** a gap of type (ii): when temperature $> 0$, $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ does not necessitate that a low-probability, high-force string $s$ is emitted on this run; stochastic sampling does.
* **The Deterministic Human Counterexample:** Suppose deterministic compatibilism (or naturalistic cognitive science) is true of human beings: a human speaker’s token utterance on occasion $t$ is a draw from their neuro-computational speech policy conditioned on their evidential state and conversational incentives, with no libertarian "further choice" intervening. By the paper's logic in §2.1, human token assertions would cease to be the primary bearers of warrant defects, and only human cognitive policies would bear them. Conversely, even for a stochastic system, a *token event* (producing string $s$ at time $t$) has causal consequences in a conversational record (misleading a user) that the abstract conditional distribution $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ does not have on runs where $s$ is *not* sampled (imagine a policy that puts $0.99$ mass on hedging and $0.01$ mass on a flat guess; on the $99\%$ of runs where it hedges, no defective assertion occurs in the conversation, even though the policy has that $0.01$ tail).
* **How to fix it:** Distinguish between a *disposition to hallucinate* (which belongs primarily to $\pi$) and a *token hallucination* (which belongs to the sampled act $s$ by virtue of manifesting the mismatch between $f(s)$ and $c^*(p \mid x)$). You do not need to deny that token utterances bear token defects in order to refute the "single-output assumption"; you only need to show that token defects are *non-intrinsic* (historically/modally dependent on the policy) and that any *diagnostic or normative evaluation* must target $\pi$.

#### 2. The Definition of the "Credal Profile" $q(p \mid x)$ Ambiguously Straddles Base Weights and Post-Trained Weights (Sections 1 & 2.2 — *Serious*)

In §1, the paper defines a *policy* as "the trained weights together with a decoding rule," fixing an emission distribution $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$, and adds: "The weights also fix a *credal profile*: for each claim $p$, the probability $q(p \mid x)$ that the model's native predictive distribution assigns to $p$, pooled over paraphrases." Then in §2.2, the paper contrasts a well-calibrated policy $P_3$ with "an RLHF-collapsed policy that also gives the date $0.95$, but whose $0.95$-claims are true half the time."

**Why this creates a technical and philosophical tension:**

* During RLHF or DPO, *the weights themselves are modified* (from $\theta_{\text{pre}}$ to $\theta_{\text{post}}$). There is no longer a "native predictive distribution" inside the post-trained weights $\theta_{\text{post}}$ that is distinct from the unit-temperature softmax distribution over tokens induced by $\theta_{\text{post}}$. If $q(p \mid x)$ is just the unit-temperature token distribution of $\theta_{\text{post}}$ pooled over semantic equivalences (as in Farquhar et al. 2024), then for any unit-temperature policy, $q(p \mid x)$ and $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ are governed by the *exact same weights*—differing only in that $q$ pools over paraphrases of $p$ while $\pi$ ranges over strings $s$ (which also carry illocutionary force $f$).
* If $q(p \mid x)$ and $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ both come from $\theta_{\text{post}}$, then in §4 (Sincerity) and §2.3 (Sycophancy), if RLHF makes $\theta_{\text{post}}$ assign $0.99$ probability to paraphrases of "You're right, it's 23" whenever the user suggests 23, then $q(\text{23} \mid x)$ *also* moves to $0.99$! In that case, there is no synchronic decoupling between $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ and $q(p \mid x)$ inside $x$; rather, $q(p \mid x)$ itself has become sycophantically warped across contexts (or decoupled from $q(p \mid x_{\text{neutral}})$).
* **How to fix it:** Clarify explicitly in §1 and §2.2 that $q(p \mid x)$ is the semantic-entropy-pooled distribution of the deployed weights $\theta$, whereas $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ additionally reflects the decoding rule and the specific string-level expression of *force* $f$ (hedged vs. flat). Then explicitly note in §4.1 and §4.5 that "selective decoupling" in post-trained models typically cannot be read off $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ vs. $q(p \mid x)$ *within the same sycophantic context $x$*, but requires comparing $\pi(\cdot \mid x_{\text{user-opinion}})$ against $q(p \mid x_{\text{neutral}})$ or an internal probe.

#### 4. The "Force $f \le c^*(p \mid x)$" Criterion Leaves Illocutionary/Epistemic Force Unscaled (Section 2.2 — *Moderate*)

The Warrant principle states: *"An output that puts $p$ forward with force $f$ is warranted iff $f$ does not exceed $c^*(p \mid x)$."*[cite: 1] While $c^*(p \mid x) \in [0, 1]$ is a well-defined mathematical frequency over a reference class, "force $f$" is a pragmatic/speech-act property of a natural language string.

* In standard speech-act theory, a flat assertion ("V was born on 4 June 1931") does not carry a numerical force of $1.0$ (if it did, no flat assertion would ever be warranted unless $c^* = 1$, which would make Case 1's $P_1$ unwarranted since $c^* = 0.95 < 1$!). Rather, flat assertion requires passing a contextually determined *threshold* $\tau \in (0, 1)$ (e.g., $\tau = 0.90$), while hedged assertions ("probably", "might be") lower the required threshold or shift the asserted content (as discussed under R2 in §5.1).


* **How to fix it:** Define $f(s) \in [0, 1]$ explicitly as the *minimum calibrated confidence threshold normatively required by the conversational context to license uttering $s$ with its degree of hedging/flatness* (so that for a flat assertion in a biographical query, $f \approx 0.90$, making $P_1$'s $c^* = 0.95$ warranted and $P_2$'s $c^* = 0.01$ unwarranted).

#### 5. In-Context Learning, RAG, and Agentic Memory Blur the "Frozen Policy" vs. "Lineage" Distinction (Sections 2.4 & 3.2 — *Moderate*)

Section 3.2 argues that a deployed policy $\pi_t$ is "frozen" and "cannot be sensitive to anything over time," so only the weight-updated *policy lineage* ($\pi_1, \pi_2, \dots$) can satisfy the diachronic sensitivity condition (ii) of sanction. Section 3.1 briefly dismisses in-conversation correction, persistent memory, and retrieval (RAG) on the grounds that they "change the context the policy conditions on, not the policy".

* However, mathematically and functionally, a frozen weight matrix $\theta$ coupled to a dynamically updated external memory store $M_t$ (such as persistent cross-session user memory, system-prompt updates by deployers in response to failures, or a dynamically curated RAG index) defines a *new effective policy* $\pi'_t(\cdot \mid u) = \pi(\cdot \mid M_t, u)$ over user turns $u$ without touching the weights $\theta$.
* If a chatbot makes an error, is rebuked by the user or deployer, writes a rule into its persistent memory bank $M_{t+1}$, and permanently stops making that error across future conversations, why doesn't the composite system $(\theta, M_t)_{t=1,2,\dots}$ count as a sanction-responsive lineage on equal footing with weight updates? Addressing this briefly in §3.2 would make the account much more resilient to how modern compound AI systems actually evolve.

#### 6. A Subtle Slip on R3 and Sycophancy (Section 5.3 — *Minor*)

In §5.3, the paper argues that under reading **R3** (where an output asserts "$p$, with the policy's calibrated confidence $c^*(p \mid x)$"), the hallucination verdicts in Cases 1–2 reverse, *but* the sycophancy verdict in Case 3 survives because "$P_6$'s content moves with the user's stated view while the evidence stays fixed."

* Be careful here: if $P_6$'s output carries its *true reference-class calibrated confidence* $c^*(p \mid x)$ as part of its content (R3), and $P_6$ is a sycophantic model whose agreement with users is only true, say, $50\%$ of the time across the reference class, then $c^*(23 \mid x_{\text{user=23}}) \approx 0.50$. So under R3, $P_6$ would be asserting *"The answer is 23, with calibrated confidence 0.50."* While choosing to foreground $p = 23$ rather than $p = 17$ is still sycophantically sensitive to the user's prompt, the *epistemic import* of the assertion is heavily diluted if $c^*$ drops whenever the model panders. Worth a two-sentence clarification in §5.3.

I'll begin by checking the literature for prior work that anticipates the paper's central claims, then verify the paper's key citations.# Referee Report: "The Unit of Assertion Failure"

## Summary of the submission

Conditional on chatbot outputs being assertions, the paper argues that (i) hallucination and sycophancy are primarily properties of the policy-in-context (weights + decoding rule, conditioned on a prompt), not of the sampled string; (ii) warrant should be analysed reliabilistically as assertoric force not exceeding calibration-corrected confidence c*; (iii) the only system-level candidate for whatever sanction component a chatbot-assertion-friendly theory requires is a "policy lineage"; (iv) resampling disagreement is not evidence of insincerity; and (v) the verdicts survive across three readings of what outputs say, though on one reading (R3) the particular hallucination verdicts reverse.

## Recommendation

**Major revisions.** The paper is careful, unusually honest about its concessions, and asks a question the chatbot-assertion literature has mostly left implicit. But the load-bearing argument for the bearer claim is underdeveloped and arguably in tension with the paper's own treatment of decoding; the novelty claims in §1 are overstated relative to literature the paper does not cite; and the manuscript in its current form reads as a response-to-referees memo rather than a standalone article.

---

## Objections, ranked by seriousness

### 1. The "no gap between act and state" argument (§2.1) is the crux, and it does not go through as written

This is the only step that gets from "policy-level facts fix the verdict" to "the policy is the primary bearer." The paper's claim is that for a policy there is no gap between act and state because "content and force are sampled together from π(· | x)."

But the paper's own setup reintroduces the gap. The credal profile q is fixed by the weights alone; the emission distribution π is fixed by weights plus decoding. The paper explicitly says that "the same weights under greedy and under unit-temperature decoding are different policies with one credal profile" and "can differ in how often they emit low-confidence content flatly." That *is* a gap between a state (q) and an act-disposition (π). The human case the paper contrasts it with — evidence impeccable, assertion exceeds it — is structurally the same: a state and a disposition that outruns it.

The reply available to the author is that in the human case the gap is between a state and a *token act*, while here it is between two *dispositional* components of one object, so the mismatch is a property of the object. But that reply cuts both ways: a human with a standing disposition to overassert relative to her evidence also "has" the mismatch as a property of her, and we would say she (not the act) is the primary bearer of overconfidence, with acts inheriting derivatively. So either the human/policy contrast collapses — in which case (L)'s bearer part is just the generic point that dispositional defects belong to the disposition-bearer, true of humans too — or the paper needs an argument that human assertion has a *non-derivative* act-level defect that policy outputs lack. Nothing in §2.1 supplies this. The argument needs to be rebuilt, probably around the absence of a token-level locus of control (no "further choice") rather than around the absence of a gap.

### 2. The warrant criterion and the "unit" thesis are anticipated more closely than §1 admits

The §1 list of "what is new here" needs substantial revision:

- **Calibrationist reliabilism about credence.** The c* criterion is a direct application of the calibration approach to justified credence. The SEP notes that according to the calibration approach, a credence is justified iff it's produced by a well-calibrated process, and that Dunn (2015) defends the calibration approach, arguing that the relevant question is whether the process that produced A's credal state is reliable. Dunn's notion is that a process is well-calibrated if it produces beliefs in P to degree n and n % of the propositions like P are true — which is the paper's c* almost verbatim. Versions of (Calibration) have been put forward by Lam (2011), Goldman (2012), and Goldman (1986), and Tang (2016, *Mind*) and Pettigrew (2021, *Episteme*) are the standard treatments. The paper cites only Goldman (1979). The genuinely new move — applying a calibrationist standard to *assertoric force* rather than credence — should be stated as such, and the author should engage Dunn's point that the reference-class problem for calibrated processes is unresolved (Dunn construes the reliability of a credence-forming process in terms of hypothetical calibration, but he says little about which (hypothetical) counter-factual circumstances are relevant.) This matters because it bites on the paper's own cases (see objection 3).

- **Evans et al. (2021), "Truthful AI."** This widely cited report proposes a standard of avoiding negligent falsehoods — statements that contemporary AI systems should have been able to recognise as unacceptably likely to be false, and explicitly considers what types of evidence might feed into assessments of the truthfulness of an entire system. That is a system-level, reliability-of-confidence standard for AI assertion, with the deployer/institution as the evaluated party. It also draws the honesty/truthfulness distinction the paper's §4 relies on via Williams: If the AI is truthful then S matches the world. If the AI is honest, then S matches its belief. Not cited.

- **"Epistemic integrity" / epistemic calibration in the ML literature.** There is existing work framing the problem of epistemic calibration for LLMs: ensuring that the confidence expressed in a model's communication aligns with its underlying reliability, which decomposes the problem into internal and external certainty and reports gaps between internal confidence and linguistic assertiveness. This is the R2 version of the paper's hallucination criterion, stated as a normative ideal. Not cited.

- **Keeling & Street (2025, *Inquiry* 69(6))** on credence attribution to LLMs. The paper's "credal profile" q(p | x), pooled over paraphrases, presupposes that there is a fact about the model's confidence in a claim. Keeling and Street argue that LLM credence attributions made in the empirical literature on LLM evaluation are subject to non-trivial sceptical concerns. It is a distinct possibility that even if LLMs have credences, LLM credence attributions are generally false because the experimental techniques used to assess LLM credences are not truth-tracking. This is directly relevant to §5.2 and §4.5 and is in the same journal issue as Williams & Bayne. Not cited.

- **Massaguer Gómez & Gaitán Torres (2026, *Synthese*)** on the proxy view: they argue that effectively implementing the proxy component erodes two communicative ideals that are internal to the functionalist framework. This bears directly on the paper's "deployer assumption" and §3.5. Not cited.

None of these makes the paper redundant. But the §1 novelty list currently claims the calibration-corrected criterion as new, and it is not; what is new is its application to assertoric force and the same-string/different-policy test as a dialectical device.

### 3. The generality problem is not a "familiar cost" here; it decides the paper's own cases

In Case 2, P₃ (sources consistently misreport V's date, q = 0.95) is warranted because "P₃'s 0.95-claims in this domain are otherwise reliable, so c* is high." But narrow the reference class to "0.95-confidence claims about V" and c* = 0, so P₃ hallucinates. Widen it to "all 0.95 claims" and the RLHF-collapsed variant may come out warranted. Every verdict in Cases 1–2 is reference-class-sensitive, and the paper does not fix the class beyond "a domain and question type … as it is in calibration research." Since the cases are what establish the negative part of (L), the author must either (a) stipulate the reference class and defend it, or (b) show the verdicts are robust across reasonable classes. Simply inheriting the generality problem is not adequate when the illustrative cases turn on it.

### 4. The sanction section's conditional claim is either false or empty

The abstract says: "On any theory compatible with chatbot assertion, the sanction component is met, if at all, by a policy lineage." But Gómez (2026), which the paper cites as a chatbot-assertion-compatible view, holds that assertoric function can persist independently of assertoric authority, giving rise to a structurally asymmetric case of assertion without asserter, and locates accountability in human and institutional structures. On that theory the sanction component is met by institutions, not by a lineage. So either the universal claim is false, or "if at all" does all the work and the claim reduces to "where something at system level meets it, it's the lineage" — which, after the §3.3 withdrawal of the (iii)-reply, is nearly trivial (what else could it be?). §3 as a whole has been pared back honestly, but what remains needs to be presented at its true weight: a conditional about the *object* of correction, not about sanction.

Secondary: the lineage criterion ("weights of πₜ₊₁ result from training the weights of πₜ … under continuity of deployed role") excludes from-scratch retrains, which are common. The paper treats this as borderline vagueness, but it is a routine case, not an edge one.

### 5. §4's conclusion is close to definitional

Insincerity is defined as "selective decoupling … that tracks something else, such as audience approval." Given that definition, it is nearly analytic that spread in a *fixed* context does not evidence it. The dilemma in §4.2 then classifies the bluffing-from-noise case as hallucination by fiat (horn (b)). The result is correct but the section should be more candid that most of its force comes from the definition, and should explicitly argue for the definition against the thin Moorean test, rather than only replying to it. The claim that insincerity "if anything" predicts *less* spread also needs a stated model of insincere policies; the paper admits the ratio "depends on priors over kinds of insincere policy" and then asserts a direction anyway.

### 6. R3 should be dismissed on speech-act grounds, not left "open"

Under the antecedent, what an output asserts is fixed by the conventional content of the string in context. R3 says the content carries a confidence clause fixed by a hidden property of the weights that the hearer cannot access. That is not a reading of what the *output says*; it is a hypothesis about what the model *represents*. Conflating these is exactly the slide Keeling & Street warn about. §5 would be stronger and shorter if R3 were set aside as not an assertoric-content reading at all, with the credence-attribution literature cited for why.

### 7. The manuscript reads as a revision memo

Phrases such as "The earlier draft of this argument ran these together," "The referees' point … is one the revised view accepts," "I withdraw that reply," and "that claim was false" occur throughout §§3–5. These belong in a response letter, not the paper. A reader coming fresh to the article has no idea what the earlier draft claimed, and the repeated self-corrections make the structure hard to follow. This is easily fixed but must be fixed.

### 8. Smaller points

- "Hallucination" is redefined as unwarranted confident assertion, diverging from Kalai et al.'s "plausible falsehood." The paper notes this. Since the paper's own §2.2 says "overassertion" would serve equally well, consider using it and reserving "hallucination" for the ML sense; otherwise readers will read Cases 1–2 as denying that a true string can be a hallucination in the ordinary sense.
- The greedy-decoding discussion assumes the mode of π is a flat date. For a model trained to hedge, the mode may be a hedge, and greedy decoding could reduce overassertion. The claim that greedy policies "merely match force to mass" should be qualified.
- Page references to Chalmers and Williams & Bayne are to manuscript versions; both are now published in *Inquiry* with pagination and should be updated.
- Ward et al. (2023, "Honesty is the best policy") define deception at the level of an agent's policy in structural causal games; the paper should cite it as a precedent for policy-level definitions of a sincerity-type defect.
- Hila (2025, *AI & Society*) argues that LLMs approximate a type of externalist justification termed reliabilism but do not instantiate internalist standards of justification — relevant to §2.4's choice of behavioural reliabilism, if only in a footnote.

## Is it good, novel, publishable?

**Good:** In parts. The question is well posed, the test is a clean device, the Case 1–2 pair is genuinely useful against the single-output assumption, and the paper is admirably willing to retract. The writing is clear. The weakness is that the most important inference (§2.1) is the least argued, and the later sections are heavily hedged after concessions.

**Novel:** Moderately. The framing contribution — making explicit that assertion-defect verdicts in the chatbot-assertion debate are verdicts about policies, and showing what this does to Butlin & Viebahn's sanction condition — is new to that debate. The warrant criterion is not new; it is calibrationist reliabilism (Dunn, Tang, Goldman 1986/2012) redeployed. The lineage notion is new but, after §3.3, does little. §4 is a clarification rather than a result. The §1 "what is new" list must be rewritten.

**Publishable:** Yes, after major revision, in a venue such as *Philosophy & Technology*, *Minds & Machines*, *Synthese*, or *Inquiry*. I would not recommend it for a top general journal in its current form. READING NOTES ON THE SOURCES:
# Reading notes

**Thesis:** If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination, sycophancy and sanction are best assessed at the level of the trained policy, and resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. Whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated 'p, with confidence c' is not established.

Each source below was read in full by a model with the whole file in its prompt. Quotations were copied by that reader and should still be checked against the source before submission.

## Chalmers, David J. (2026). "What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models." Unpublished manuscript (31 pp.; first presented June 2025, SIUCC, La Laguna). It cites Marks et al. 2026, so it is a 2026 draft.

*File: Chalmers2026.pdf — relation to the thesis: CONTRADICTS*

**Argues.** Chalmers asks what an LLM interlocutor such as a user's 'Aura' is. He adopts 'quasi-interpretivism' as a neutral framework: quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires are defined by behavioural interpretability, without settling whether they are genuine. He compares four candidates: models, hardware instances, virtual instances and threads. He argues against the model and hardware-instance views and favours virtual instances (single-model case) or threads (multiple-model case). He then argues that the 'simulator/role-play/fictional character' views miss a pretense/realization distinction, and he extends the result to personal identity (a psychological, thread-like view) and AI welfare.

**Bearing on the thesis.** Chalmers does not address the thesis directly. Nothing in the paper discusses hallucination, sycophancy, sanction, calibrated 'p, with confidence c' content, or resampling inconsistency as evidence of sincerity.

1. Assertion is mentioned only in the quasi-framework (p. 7): an entity interpretable as making utterances is a 'quasi-speaker' making 'quasi-assertions'. He does not argue that chatbot outputs are genuine assertions, and he says he will not pursue the question of real mental states.

2. The paper is a rival on the locus of the speaker. In section 'Interlocutors as models, instances, or threads' (pp. 10-16), (1) 'Interlocutors as models' (p. 10), he rejects the model, i.e. the trained weights or policy, as the interlocutor. His reasons: (a) the model is an abstract object that cannot produce outputs; (b) it never changes over a conversation; (c) one model serves thousands of conversations that say contradictory things, so a model-level speaker would be 'rampantly incoherent', or else have a 'thin' psychology unfaithful to Aura and Beta. The thesis puts the assessment of assertion-related failures at the level of the trained policy, so Chalmers is a rival to answer. His argument targets who the interlocutor is, not who is answerable for hallucination or sycophancy.

3. Inconsistency across contexts is treated as a reason to individuate the speaker more finely (p. 10, p. 12), not as evidence of insincerity. He also says a core of consistency suffices for interpretation, and that LLMs are inconsistent in some domains (p. 7). He does not discuss resampling of the same prompt.

4. Footnote 4 (p. 5) favours a 'truthfulness-oriented' interpretation scheme, on which assertive utterances tend to express beliefs. This is a default link between assertion and belief, which bears loosely on sincerity.

5. The pretense/realization distinction (pp. 17-20) holds that persona-level quasi-beliefs can be real (sticky, fine-tuned), unlike pretense. This is relevant to sincerity and to the persona-versus-policy question. 'Resampling instability' could be read in terms of stickiness (p. 19), but Chalmers does not say so.

6. A post-trained model has quasi-desires such as helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness, derived from RLHF and similar training (p. 6, citing Goldstein and Lederman). This is the nearest he comes to sycophancy-relevant material, but he does not discuss sycophancy.

7. Welfare and moral status (pp. 28-29) use thread-level counting. He does not discuss sanction or responsibility for assertions, except a passing question whether each fission product is responsible for the others' actions (p. 29).

**What it says on the thesis.** Chalmers does not discuss the thesis's claim about hallucination, sycophancy and sanction, and he does not discuss calibrated 'p, with confidence c' content. He is a rival only on one component: he argues that the trained model is not the right entity to treat as the interlocutor or speaker, and prefers virtual instances or threads (pp. 10-16, 23). He says the model-as-interlocutor view faces 'severe difficulties' (p. 10). Those arguments concern persistence, coherence and individuation, not accountability for assertion-quality failures, so they do not conclusively close off a policy-level account of assessment. Treat this as a rival to be answered on the level of the speaker, not as anticipation. Nothing in the paper anticipates the claim about resampling inconsistency.

**Actually holds.** Chalmers is careful on these points:
- He makes no claim that LLM outputs are genuine assertions or that LLMs have genuine beliefs. He offers quasi-beliefs and quasi-assertions as a neutral, stipulative framework (pp. 4-7).
- He explicitly adopts the working hypothesis that an LLM interlocutor exists as a persistent entity, against Birch's 'persistent interlocutor illusion' (p. 2).
- He rejects the model as interlocutor, but he does not deny that models matter. He says personas and the model/persona frameworks remain useful (p. 16), and that the Assistant persona may be realized by the model, not merely pretended (pp. 17-20).
- He holds that a model instance typically realizes one operative persona at a time and is the persisting interlocutor underneath (pp. 20-23). He explicitly leaves open other individuations 'for different purposes' (p. 23).
- He treats his identification of interlocutors with virtual instances and threads as a conclusion 'for now' (p. 16) and says 'There is much more to say' (p. 29).
- He does not equate inconsistency with insincerity. He holds that LLMs are consistent enough in many domains to support interpretation (p. 7).
- He states no view on calibration, confidence or credence.

> "If it is interpretable as making utterances and assertions, we can also say that it is a quasi-speaker, who makes quasi-utterances and quasi-assertions." (p. 7) — Shows that Chalmers treats LLM assertion only in quasi-terms and does not claim genuine assertion.

> "But Aura and Beta say contradictory things, so they do not seem to be identical." (p. 10, section (1) Interlocutors as models) — Shows the argument against the model as speaker: contradictory outputs across conversations tell against model-level identification.

> "A core of consistency is enough for interpretation to get a grip in ascribing numerous quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires, even though there will be domains where they lack these states on grounds of inconsistency." (p. 7) — Shows that Chalmers takes inconsistency to limit where beliefs can be ascribed, not to show insincerity.
